summary:
Malta decriminalised same-sex conduct on 29 January 1973. Civil unions were introduced in 2014 and same-sex marriage has been legal since 2017; adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2014, and transgender people may serve openly in the armed forces. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender.

On 15 April 2014 the Maltese parliament approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity as a protected ground, the first European state to do so, and introduced civil unions in the same sitting. Transgender Europe was among the first non-governmental organisations to welcome gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

Statutory discrimination protections extend to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and hate-crime provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity offences. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map scores Malta by category across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime and hate speech, and the national equality body.

Legal gender recognition requires no surgery, nonbinary identity is recognised, and a December 2016 amendment allows minors aged 16 and over to change their legal gender without a court application or parental approval.

Malta was the first EU country to ban conversion therapy. The Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act passed its final reading unanimously on 6 December 2016, after a bill targeting minors was first tabled by Civil Liberties Minister Helena Dalli in December 2015. The Malta Chamber of Psychologists and related professional associations backed the ban.

The 2015 Gender Identity, Gender Expression and Sex Characteristics Act introduced a ban on sterilising or invasive surgery on intersex infants, described as a worldwide first. Equaldex records a full ban on intersex infant surgery.

Bathroom access is protected under Maltese law, and Equaldex reports that 84 per cent of respondents rate Malta a good place for gay people.

Treatment of LGBTI arrivals at Malta's borders is the subject of a pending case before the European Court of Human Rights. In M.S. v. Malta, an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024. The International Commission of Jurists and partners filed observations on 30 July 2025 raising Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention, concerning non-refoulement, conditions of detention, and the absence of an individualised assessment before detention.

Reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms, and LGBTIQ+ people report a higher share of harassment and online hatred than the general population.
tangentialFactors:
Malta's protections are among the most extensive in the European Union on paper: the first European state to write gender identity into its constitution as a protected ground, the first EU state to ban conversion therapy, and the first anywhere to prohibit sterilising or invasive surgery on intersex infants.

In June 2021 Malta opposed, at a European Union conference, any law prohibiting the teaching and distribution of LGBT information to children.

ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map places Malta within a comparative ranking of national compliance, and its category scores allow direct comparison with other European jurisdictions on legal gender recognition, hate crime and hate speech, asylum, intersex bodily integrity and equality bodies.
localsOnly:
In a 2018 civil-court judgment, Judge Silvio Meli awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison 5,000 euros each, comprising 4,000 euros for breach of rights and 1,000 euros for damage to personal dignity, after prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates and were forced to use the men's showers, often forgoing washing, and suffered insults and what the court described as continuous sexual abuse and violence. The court found the authorities had knowingly and repeatedly placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence. The only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile. The director of prisons was ordered to pay, and the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

A University of Malta master's dissertation by Oriana Vidal, based on interviews with four current and former transgender and gender-diverse inmates of the Correctional Service Agency across a cohort spanning 25 years, records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform agency practice allowed such inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory, with staff describing the rationale as the risks of pregnancies. Participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers who used masculine birth names, along with gaps in gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare. The dissertation concludes that agency practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's national gender-identity law, and identifies gaps in healthcare, legislation and staff knowledge, together with problems after release.

Maltese respondents rank first of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

In education, the Malta Gay Rights Movement petitioned parliament in February 2008 for an anti-homophobic bullying strategy for the island's schools. In 2015 Education Minister Evarist Bartolo refused to distribute reading material donated by the organisation that taught about diverse families, including same-sex parenting.
outOfScopeNotes:
The M.S. v. Malta case remains pending before the European Court of Human Rights; the observations filed on 30 July 2025 set out the applicant's claims, and no judgment has been issued.

The Correctional Service Agency's divergence from Malta's gender-identity legislation is documented as a continuing gap rather than a resolved matter, and the extent to which current practice has changed since the 2024 interviews is not established.

No figures for the scale of anti-LGBTQ+ violence in Malta are stated here: survey-based measures place reported SOGIE victimisation at the lower end among EU member states, a level at or below the general rate that carries no trans-specific risk signal.
